changes.before: Change twice(3) to twice(2.5). What occurs?
changes.after: Limit the types a template accepts with a concept.

before: A concept is a compile-time constraint. <concepts> supplies std::integral, which accepts integral types such as int but not double. template<std::integral T> constrains the type parameter.
Constraints improve which calls are permitted; they do not prove all runtime inputs safe. This doubling example uses small values whose result fits int. Unchecked signed overflow is not allowed.
Calling twice with 2.5 fails constraint checking instead of quietly truncating it. There is no successful runtime result for that changed program.

Expected output or behavior: 6
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Try an unsigned integer literal 3u, keeping the arithmetic safely within its range. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A concept is a named requirement checked before the program runs. It limits which types a template can accept.
<concepts> provides std::integral. It accepts integer types such as int and rejects floating-point types such as double. template<std::integral T> applies that requirement to T.
The compiler works out T from the input, then checks the requirement. A double input fails this requirement, so that call is rejected before execution.
The program prints 6. Three has type int, which meets std::integral. The function adds three to itself.
The concept checks the type, not whether every possible calculation is safe. A signed integer result must still fit its type's range. This example uses small values that fit.
